venture.summary: As an increasing number of AI assistants flood the market, the founder of Ollie, an assistant that respected its users' privacy, says it will be shutting down in a week.

venture.headline: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
venture.summary: Big Tech is pouring billions into AI infrastructure, but mounting debt, negative cash flow, and growing investor skepticism are raising questions about the sustainability of the AI spending boom.

research.headline: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
research.summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them.

research.headline: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
research.summary: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private.

research.headline: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
research.summary: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation.

research.headline: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
research.summary: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks.

research.headline: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
research.summary: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence.

titans.headline: Sam Altman sympathizes with mathematicians, but says OpenAI’s math onslaught won’t stop
titans.summary: After months of bombarding mathematicians with a relentless stream of AI-generated results, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he sympathizes with researchers struggling to make sense of it all. But he has no intention of stopping - and hints there could be much more to come from the company's stockpile of discoveries.

regulatory.headline: FTC Staff Warn 25 Healthcare Marketers Against Deceptive Advertising Terms
regulatory.summary: Federal Trade Commission staff are sending warning letters to 25 companies that market or generate sales leads for healthcare plans during open enrollment season. The letters cite FTC enforcement actions against alleged violators and urge marketers not to deceive consumers regarding advertised plan terms.

regulatory.headline: FTC removes 19 imposter websites and secures over $80 million in redress
regulatory.summary: The Federal Trade Commission released highlights detailing its ongoing efforts to combat impersonation scams. Since its Impersonation Rule took effect in 2024, the agency has removed 19 FTC-imposter websites. These enforcement actions have yielded more than $80 million in consumer redress.

regulatory.headline: FTC Orders Nine Companies to Detail Personal Data Pricing Methods
regulatory.summary: The Federal Trade Commission ordered nine major airlines, ride-sharing companies, and food-delivery firms to submit detailed operational information. The regulatory inquiry aims to analyze how these companies utilize personal data to determine prices and set worker compensation.

regulatory.headline: FTC and State Regulators Sue Toast Inc. Over Deceptive Fees
regulatory.summary: The Federal Trade Commission and multiple state authorities filed a lawsuit against restaurant software firm Toast Inc. The agencies allege that Toast deceptively touts costs and customer support while engaging in unauthorized fee and cancellation practices.

regulatory.headline: PlayPower Abandons Proposed Acquisition of Rival Playground Manufacturer BCI Burke
regulatory.summary: Platinum Equity and its portfolio company PlayPower abandoned their proposed acquisition of rival playground manufacturer BCI Burke. Federal Trade Commission Bureau of Competition Director Daniel Guarnera issued an official statement following the announcement. The transaction was terminated amid regulatory involvement from the FTC.

frontier.headline: Entanglement diagnostics of stochastic-resetting steady states: theory and measurement on superconducting qubits
frontier.summary: Stochastic resetting drives quantum systems into nonequilibrium stationary states unreachable under uninterrupted unitary evolution, and their entanglement depends on whether the reset history is resolved or averaged over. We study this interplay in the transverse-field Ising chain, deriving closed-form results for two qubits and evaluating chains of up to 12 qubits exactly. In the two-qubit system, these closed-form results show that phase matching between energy eigenstates produces resonances, and their visibility in the stationary state is determined by the symmetry of the reset state.

frontier.headline: Left-Handed Transmission Lines for the Dynamical Casimir Effect
frontier.summary: Left-handed (LH) superconducting transmission lines, built with series capacitors and shunt inductors instead of the series inductors and shunt capacitors of a conventional right-handed (RH) line, have a spectrum with a nonzero lower band edge and modes that become sparse at high frequencies. We study the dynamical Casimir effect in a LH line terminated by a flux-modulated SQUID and compare it with an RH line built from the same elements and with a long coplanar waveguide terminated by the same SQUID. We derive the quantum Hamiltonian and show that the coupling between two modes factorizes into their amplitudes at the SQUID.

frontier.headline: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
frontier.summary: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.

frontier.headline: Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
frontier.summary: Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive.

frontier.headline: Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
frontier.summary: A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead.

industry.headline: Pornhub Stars Want to Teach You How to Make Dinner
industry.summary: Faced with censorship and anti-porn laws, the adult site is encouraging creators to embrace cooking, gaming, podcasting, and other safe-for-work content.

voices.headline: Is the AI Boom Depressing the Rest of the Economy?
voices.summary: Over the past four years, Dallas, the beating heart of the U.S. energy economy, has become the beating heart of the U.S. That’s thanks to its cheap land, friendly regulatory posture, liquid labor market, excellent transportation infrastructure, and ample grid connectivity.

voices.headline: Can Democracy Survive the Next Financial Crash?
voices.summary: T he bailout clock is ticking. In September, Oracle invoked “force majeure” to delay paying debt on a data center, which led to a drop in the corporation’s stock price. This month, OpenAI significantly cut its revenue projections; CoreWeave, a heavily leveraged data-center company, saw its share price plunge; and investors began racing to buy credit-default swaps to protect their portfolios.

voices.headline: The Currency of the Journal Article Is Collapsing
voices.summary: Weak scholarship was once easy to spot at a glance: The signs included bad writing, a lack of relevant citations, and little engagement with previous scholarship, such as a paper that promised a “novel” conceptual framework without acknowledging the many other papers making similar claims. As an associate editor of a bioethics journal, I’d make a quick “desk reject” decision and not send these articles for peer review, which effectively killed any hope of publication. Now I can say: AI is affecting every part of academic publishing.

voices.headline: The Limits of Trump’s Midterm Trickery
voices.summary: For the first time in modern American history, a sitting president is seeking to wield the force of the state to secure an electoral victory for his party. The Trump administration has attempted to undermine the widespread use of mail-in voting; demanded that states hand over voter rolls; threatened to prosecute state and local election officials; refused to rule out the idea of deploying troops or federal agents to polling places; and publicized the dramatic arrests of small numbers of people accused of voting or registering to vote as noncitizens. Many of these efforts have made little headway—either because of the administration’s incompetence, the stubborn lack of factual evidence behind President Trump’s claims of voter fraud, the federal government’s lack of legal authority, or the refusal of courts to go along with Trump’s plans.

voices.headline: The Variety Bag Has Ruined Halloween
voices.summary: All Halloween candy is the same now. Nothing stands out, apart from the quantity of candy dumped out on the floor back home. Every house seems to buy a variety bag of seemingly random candy, and consequently every stop metes out a little more of the same treats as the previous one did or the next one will.
